title: Raila v. United States (2d Cir. 2004)
summary: The Second Circuit held that the postal-matter exception did not bar a personal-injury suit arising from a package negligently placed near a doorstep.
notes: The Supreme Court reached the same result two years later in Dolan v. United States Postal Service, 546 U.S. 481 (2006), citing Raila with approval and holding that the postal exception covers loss, delay or damage to mail but not injuries caused by negligently placed mail; Raila was written by then-Judge Sotomayor.

sections.Parties: Lenore Raila sued the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act for injuries allegedly caused by a postal employee’s negligence. The government asserted sovereign immunity under the postal-matter exception.
sections.Material Facts: Raila slipped on a package left just below her front doorstep. The Federal Tort Claims Act broadly waived immunity for specified employee torts under circumstances in which a private person would be liable under applicable local law. Section 2680(b) preserved immunity for claims arising from loss, miscarriage, or negligent transmission of letters or postal matter. The dispute concerned whether negligent placement causing bodily injury fell within that exception.
sections.Procedural History: The District of Connecticut dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, relying on the ordinary meaning of transmission and decisions applying the exception through delivery. Raila appealed. A Second Circuit panel of Cardamone, Sotomayor, and Katzmann unanimously reversed. The decision removed this jurisdictional bar and allowed the claim to proceed; it did not establish negligence or award damages.
sections.Issue: Did negligent transmission include every negligent act occurring during mail delivery, or only failures associated with loss, delay, misdelivery, or damage to the mail and resulting harm?
sections.Holding: The exception did not bar Raila’s slip-and-fall claim. The district court erred in dismissing for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
sections.Reasoning: The panel began with text in statutory context. A broad reading could absorb virtually all postal negligence, while the neighboring terms loss and miscarriage pointed toward a narrower category of mail-service failures. Noscitur a sociis therefore supported reading transmission in light of its companions. Kosak’s discussion of the Act’s purpose and narrower wording of the postal exception reinforced that reading, including the recognized liability for negligently operated postal vehicles. Limited legislative history linked the exception to losses for which registration could provide protection. Hypotheticals exposed arbitrary distinctions between injury from a flying package and a truck, or from a liquid parcel and a janitor’s puddle. Katzmann attributes the panel’s result to congressional purpose and constrained interpretation, while noting that Congress could amend the statute if it wanted broader immunity.

topics.lrs-k-noscitur: The panel read negligent transmission alongside loss and miscarriage to identify a common class of mail-related injury.
topics.lrs-k-purposivism: The panel compared the government’s reading with the Act’s treatment of ordinary postal-employee torts and its protective postal exception.
topics.lrs-k-sovereign-immunity: The case interprets a statutory exception within a broad tort waiver rather than assuming every ambiguity requires maximal immunity.
topics.lrs-k-absurdity: The panel tested competing readings against contrasting package, vehicle, and puddle hypotheticals.
topics.lrs-k-ftca-postal: Raila is a direct construction of the § 2680(b) postal-matter exception, which the atlas already lists as a rule.
